source: Europe PMC citation list for Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011), PMID 21561605
finding: Forward-citation list pulled this session: 112 citing records in Europe PMC (2014-2026). I scanned the titles for direct replications of the bead contrast (ambiguous vs unambiguous evidence, free play). None is titled or described as a replication or a failed replication. The closest are conceptual extensions with different tasks.
numbers: 112 citing records; 0 titled as a direct replication; about 10 conceptual extensions (van Schijndel 2015, McCormack 2016, Lapidow and Walker 2020, Koksal 2021, Moeller 2022, Bramley 2022, Chu and Schulz 2023, Lapidow and Bonawitz 2023, Siegel 2021, Ruggeri 2019).
limits: Title scan only for most records. Europe PMC misses non-indexed work (CogSci proceedings, OSF, Many Labs). No registry hit was checked. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors.
agent_relevance: The Cook base-rate contrast stays a single-lab result. Treat 45-50% vs 5% as an existence proof, not a calibrated rate.

source: Lapidow and Walker (2020) Informative experimentation in intuitive science: children select and learn from their own causal interventions. Cognition
finding: Conceptual extension, abstract only. Four- to six-year-olds chose between two interventions on a gear system. One (remove one gear so the other is seen alone) shows the true structure. They clearly preferred it and made judgments that fit the outcome. In Experiment 2 the informative action was less likely to give a pleasing effect, and the preference held. Experiment 3 ruled out low-level strategies.
numbers: Ages 4-6. Exact N and percentages not read (abstract only).
quote: children demonstrated a clear preference for the action that revealed the true causal structure
limits: Forced choice between two options, not free play, so the informative action is handed to the child. It does not test the unambiguous-evidence contrast, so it cannot show restraint.
agent_relevance: Supports reading A for gap 4: when the isolating action is on the menu, young children pick it. The 5% in Cook then reflects not generating or not wanting it in free play, more than inability. A menu of candidate tests at S7 is likely to help.

source: Moeller, Sodian, Sobel (2022) Developmental trajectories in diagnostic reasoning: understanding data are confounded develops independently of choosing informative interventions. Front. Psychol.
finding: Recognising that evidence is confounded and choosing a controlled test were unrelated in 3- to 6-year-olds. Children chose the controlled test above chance in the two-variable trials and only marginally in the three-variable trials.
numbers: N=57 (mean 65.1 months, range 41-81; 5 excluded). Two-variable controlled-test choice: both trials 46% (26/57), one trial 40% (23/57), none 14% (8/57); vs chance chi2(2)=13.49, p=.001, w=.49. Three-variable: chi2(2)=4.78, p=.09, w=.29. Relevant justifications 38% of the time.
limits: Forced-choice task with explicit judgments, not free play. Small sample, one lab.
agent_relevance: Competing reading to Cook: choosing an isolating test does not need an explicit sense that the evidence is confounded. A gate that depends on the model saying 'this is ambiguous' may be the wrong trigger. A code-computed tie check does not rely on that sense.

source: Siegel, Magid, Pelz, Tenenbaum, Schulz (2021) Children's exploratory play tracks the discriminability of hypotheses. Nat. Commun. (full text re-read for N)
finding: Resolves the N question. The abstract says N = 160 (mean 5y4m). The Methods say 184 children were recruited (mean 5;2, range 3;0-8;6) and 16 were excluded, so 168 were analysed. Experiments 4-7 each had 24 children, and 7 x 24 = 168 fits. The abstract figure 160 does not match.
numbers: Abstract N=160. Methods: 184 recruited - 16 excluded = 168. More exploration for harder discriminations: Exp 4 19/24 (79%), Exp 5 21/24 (85%), Exp 6 18/24 (75%), Exp 7 19/24 (79%). Exp 7 and the 16-contrast analysis were preregistered (OSF).
limits: The exclusion reasons are printed with trailing numbers (12, 3, 4, 1) that sum to 20 if they are counts, so they may be reference markers; I could not tell. Museum sample, ages 3-8.
agent_relevance: Use N=168 (about 7 x 24) in notes and flag the abstract slip. The preregistered Exp 7 is the one pre-registered support for exploration scaling with how hard hypotheses are to tell apart.

source: Pan, Xie, Wilson (2025) Large language models think too fast to explore effectively (Little Alchemy 2, full text)
finding: Resolves the R1 question. The main text says both o1 and DeepSeek-R1 beat humans (o1 177 elements, R1 85, humans 42 within 500 trials; 51 over all trials). The abstract names only o1. Appendix C.2 calls R1 near human-level and below o1. The paper is not consistent with itself.
numbers: 500 trials per LLM; 29,493 human players. Elements found: LLaMA3.1-8B 9, LLaMA3.1-70B 25, GPT-4o 35, R1 85, o1 177, humans 42. t vs humans: o1 9.71 (p<.001), R1 3.40 (reported p<.027, odd for that t), GPT-4o -5.48, 70B -6.39, 8B -28.12. Temperature x uncertainty beta=2.911; temperature x empowerment beta=0.196 (p=.286).
limits: One game. R1 was described as a quick investigation in the appendix. Only o1 had an empowerment weight above humans.
agent_relevance: Keep K16 contested and correct the record: do not cite R1 as clearly above humans.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning (per-condition tables)
finding: Per-condition Zendo scores (out of 8 test scenes, mean over 5 seeds). Choosing experiments by code-computed information gain beats asking the LLM for a good experiment and beats random. Reranking matters more than who proposes: a hand-coded random proposer did about as well as the LLM proposer once information gain reranked.
numbers: Online fuzzy / online hard: LLM-chosen experiments 4.52 / 4.72; random 5.03 / 5.84; InfoGain 5.35 / 6.55. Candidates considered 1 / 5 / 10 with random proposer: 5.84 / 6.23 / 6.55. ReAct-style direct LLM 4.60 of 8. Humans 5.26 of 8. ActiveACRE task solving: online hard 0.35 vs batch with refinement 0.10-0.15. Batch inference plateaus after 15 hypotheses (1 LLM call); online plateaus after 75 (5 calls).
limits: GPT-4 Turbo class (2023-24), GPT-3.5 for code translation. Compute is counted in LLM calls, not tokens, so it is not an equal-token test. Row alignment in Table 3/4 read from a PDF text dump.
agent_relevance: Best direct number for gap 5: code-side selection adds about 1.8 of 8 scenes over LLM-chosen tests on this task with older models. Not shown at modern scale or at equal tokens.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Language model agents are poor causal explorers (COLM) - appendix Table 1 and C.2/C.5 re-read
finding: Exploration progress at end of episode (1 = one hypothesis left) is close to ceiling for random play at 4 objects, so gains are hard to see there. At 8 objects random reaches 0.944 (OR) and 0.877 (AND). LM rows range 0.812-0.999 (OR) and 0.798-0.935 (AND), and two of four LM rows have negative random-normalised progress. Higher reasoning effort in the o-mini series lagged lower effort in the AND setting. Hypothesis sampling with 16/32/64/96 initial hypotheses improved Q&A and removed the OR/AND gap, read from a figure.
numbers: 4 objects: random 0.968 OR / 0.964 AND; oracle 1.000. 8 objects: random 0.944 / 0.877; oracle 1.000. Normalised progress from -2.342 to 0.983 with SD up to 6.5 (very noisy). No table value for the Q&A gain.
limits: Row labels were scrambled in the PDF text, so I did not assign values to named models. Figure 9b values are not printed. 2025-era GPT-4o and DeepSeek models. Equal tokens not controlled.
agent_relevance: The enumerate-and-eliminate gain is clear for the AND case, but the exploration-progress table is noisy and often near random. Keep the claim at 'reduces the disjunctive bias' and drop any size claim until a table value is found.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists - Passive Proposer design re-read
finding: Passive Proposers planned tests but were shown the outcomes of a matched Active Explorer's tests, not outcomes of their own proposals. Their object identification in conjunctive worlds was 0.12, below Passive Observers (0.45) and Active Explorers (0.69). The authors read this as needing contingent outcomes. The design mixes two things: no control over the evidence, and outcomes that do not match the proposer's own plan.
numbers: 102 Passive Observers and 102 Passive Proposers, each yoked to one Active Explorer. Conjunctive object ID: proposer 0.12, observer 0.45, active 0.69. Rule selection: 0.57, 0.69, 0.82. LLMs were run only as active sequential testers; there is no LLM batch-plan arm.
limits: No condition lets a proposer see its own outcome without acting. The mismatch between plan and observed outcome is a plausible cause of the low 0.12, and the paper does not separate it.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open for LLMs: no study compares an interleaved test-then-choose loop with a batch plan at equal tokens. Design note: a loop that plans several tests and reads results out of order resembles the Proposer, which did worst.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to falsify - Blicket Table 4 and token table re-read
finding: Think-in-Opposites on the blicket task gives a big gain only for Qwen3-32B in thinking mode. Other thinking models gain little. Non-thinking models do not gain on average. On the Wason task it costs extra tokens in several thinking models.
numbers: Blicket task success (192 episodes), baseline to TiO. Thinking: Qwen3-8B 0.32 to 0.40; 14B 0.50 to 0.61; 32B 0.57 to 0.86; R1-Llama-70B 0.41 to 0.43; QwQ-32B 0.80 to 0.82. Non-thinking: 8B 0.11 to 0.19; 14B 0.25 to 0.20; 32B 0.64 to 0.56; Llama-3.3-70B 0.78 to 0.82. Wason tokens per turn, thinking: 8B 1088 to 1716 (+58%); 14B 1179 to 1332 (+13%); 32B 1030 to 1450 (+41%); R1-70B 958 to 1073 (+12%); QwQ 1758 to 1465 (-17%). Non-thinking tokens per turn about the same (8B: 8.4 vs 8.4).
limits: PDF column alignment was messy; values were taken from row order and agree with the earlier note (0.57 to 0.86, 0.64 to 0.56). Not equal-token. No code check that the proposed test splits the rules.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: 'helps in thinking mode only' holds for 32B but the other thinking models gain only 0.02-0.11, and non-thinking results are mixed (+0.08, -0.05, -0.08, +0.04). The 32B gain also comes with about 41% more tokens on Wason. A code check on test quality is the next thing to test.

source: Alderete, Benthall, Xu, Xing (2026) Separable pathways for causal reasoning (full text re-read)
finding: Blicket hidden-moderator task with Sonnet 4.5 as the model. A context graph (typed state machine, 4 states) and code-side dynamic behaviours (monitors that expand the hypothesis space) were added separately. The context graph drove most of the reasoning quality after a rule switch; the behaviours fixed premature commitment. Base was not clearly worse than the full scaffold in raw accuracy.
numbers: 1,085 trials. Combined runs, easy post-switch rule (110 per arm): raw accuracy Base 96/110 (87.3%), CG 85/110 (77.3%), CG+DB 98/110 (89.1%); CG+DB vs CG Fisher p=0.015 one-tailed, BF10=100.4. Reasoning-eligible: Base 81/110 (73.6%), CG 75/110 (68.2%), CG+DB 96/110 (87.3%). Conjunctive post-switch (CDE): CG+DB 100% vs Base 80%. Context graph accounts for 94% of the reasoning-quality gain. One powered comparison showed no reliable advantage (+10 pp, p=.276).
limits: One model family; the scaffold also uses Haiku for monitors. Exploration depth and trap structure confound raw accuracy. Runs 01-02 were dropped for ceiling and a bug, and the benchmark was tuned over runs.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of a code-side gate on a blicket task. The gains are against the context-graph arm, and Base is nearly as good in raw accuracy, so a gate is not free. Supports separating 'when to test' (monitor) from 'how well to reason after' (graph).

source: Modelled break-even for gate vs always-split vs never-split (this session, toy simulation, no LLM calls)
finding: Simulated an episode where a splitting test resolves a rule tie for certain and each ordinary test resolves it with probability 0.2 (3 tries). Policies: never-split, always-split, code gate (exact check of the rule list for a tie, small cost) and a model-judge gate (recall 0.5, false alarm 0.1). The result follows from the assumptions and is not an LLM measurement. A code gate beats always-split when gate cost < (1 - tie rate) x split cost. Never-split beats an expensive gate when ties are rare.
numbers: Split test 300 tokens, ordinary test 300, gate 20 or 150. Accuracy per 1k tokens at tie rate 0.1/0.3/0.5/0.9. Gate 20: never 12.7/4.0/2.0/0.8; always 3.3 at all rates; code gate 19.8/9.1/5.9/3.5; model-judge 9.8/4.8/3.0/1.6. Gate 150: code gate 5.5/4.2/3.3/2.4 (vs never 12.7 at tie 0.1). Accuracy: always and code gate 1.000; never 0.948/0.855/0.747/0.542; model-judge 0.975/0.926/0.875/0.768.
limits: Assumptions are mine: perfect split test, perfect code gate, fixed costs. Says nothing about whether a real LLM reads ties correctly.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 closed as a design argument and open as a measurement. Keep the trigger only if it can be computed in code for much less than a split test. If ties are rare and the gate costs about half a test, skip it.

source: Search for an LLM version of the Cook et al. (2011) base-rate contrast (this session)
finding: Searches (web search, arXiv API, Europe PMC citations) found no paper that gives an LLM the ambiguous vs unambiguous contrast and counts how often it runs the single splitting test. Nearest items: Jhaveri 2026 (falsifying tests, not triggered by ambiguity), GX-Chen 2025 (ambiguous inference preference, not test choice), Samiei 2026.
numbers: 0 direct LLM tests found. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited.
limits: Absence of evidence from limited search tools. A very recent paper could be missed.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: it needs our own toy run with real model calls. The simulation gives only the expected shape.

source: Prompt-narrowing search: no LLM analogue of Bonawitz et al. (2011) found (this session); Lee et al. (2025) 2412.13422; Xiong (2026) 2605.05851
finding: Searches for an LLM study where a stated hypothesis or worked example narrows exploration, counted as distinct candidates, found none. Related: Lee et al. (2025, NAACL) report that sampled hypotheses are often near-duplicates and that giving each sample a different concept as a hint raises diversity. Xiong (2026) finds LLM hypothesis behaviour depends strongly on prompt and examples, and that models generate simpler hypotheses than they judge correct when evaluating.
numbers: No numbers read; abstracts and search summaries only.
limits: A distinct hint per sample widens the output. A hint that states one answer, which Bonawitz tested, is the opposite design.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Cheap test: ask for N candidate tests with and without a stated hypothesis and count distinct classes with a code classifier.

source: Sobel, Benton, Finiasz, Taylor, Weisberg (2022) The influence of children's first action when learning causal structure from exploratory play. Cognitive Development
finding: From a search snippet and Crossref metadata only. Ages 4-7. Children who generated the data needed to disambiguate the structure were more likely to learn it. Children showed some systematic play but did not generally isolate variables to test single hypotheses.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Snippet only. It may qualify Cook: spontaneous isolation may not be widespread when the task is a full causal structure.
agent_relevance: A candidate boundary condition. It needs a real read before use.

source: Ruggeri, Swaboda, Sim, Gopnik (2019) Shake it baby, but only when needed: preschoolers adapt their exploratory strategies to the information structure of the task. Cognition
finding: Abstract only. Training on the likelihood structure before the task changed which exploratory action preschoolers chose. 3- and 4-year-olds shook first more often when the egg was equally likely in any box than when it was skewed. Five-year-olds did not adapt unless the link between the training and the game was highlighted.
numbers: Exact N not read.
limits: Different task (finding a hidden object), not isolating variables.
agent_relevance: Supports reading C for gap 4: information about the task structure given in-session changes which probing action children choose. For the agent, supplying the structure (rule list) at S7 should shape the choice.

source: van Schijndel, Visser, van Bers, Raijmakers (2015) Preschoolers perform more informative experiments after observing theory-violating evidence. JECP
finding: Abstract only. Conceptual extension in a shadow-size domain. All children who saw conflicting evidence ran an unconfounded informative experiment at the start of play, against half of those who saw confirming evidence. The experiments targeted the dimension at the core of the child's own theory.
numbers: All (100%) vs about half (50%). N not read.
limits: Theory violation, not tied evidence. Different domain and lab.
agent_relevance: Independent-lab support for 'conflict triggers the clean test' (K06). Gives a second trigger for S7: a contradiction with the held rule, not only a tie.

source: Bramley, Jones, Gureckis, Ruggeri (2022) Children's failure to control variables may reflect adaptive decision-making. Psychon. Bull. Rev.
finding: Abstract only. 7- to 13-year-olds adjusted whether they controlled variables to how many causes were likely (causal sparsity). Controlling variables is not always the most efficient strategy.
numbers: n=104. Effect sizes not read.
limits: School-age children, not preschoolers.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for always-split: when many causes are plausible, isolating one at a time can cost more than testing groups. Fits a gate that splits only when few rules are tied.

source: Koksal, Sodian, Legare (2021) Young children's metacognitive awareness of confounded evidence. JECP
finding: Abstract only. 5- and 6-year-olds asked for more information with confounded than unconfounded evidence, and nearly half referred to several candidate causes when explaining.
limits: Verbal task, and older than Cook's 4-5-year-olds.
agent_relevance: Detection of ambiguity exists by 5-6. Together with Moeller 2022 (no link to choosing a controlled test) it suggests detection and action can be separate steps.

source: Legare (2012) Exploring explanation: explaining inconsistent evidence informs exploratory, hypothesis-testing behavior in young children. Child Development
finding: Abstract only (Crossref). In 2- to 6-year-olds (N=80), the kind of explanation given for an inconsistent outcome predicted the kind of exploratory testing and the number of new hypotheses. This was not so for consistent outcomes.
limits: Does not give the informative action for free or train isolation first. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: I found no study that trains isolation first and then repeats the Cook contrast. Legare shows inconsistency plus explaining shapes testing, which fits learning in session more than a fixed skill.

source: From Curiosity to Competence: how world models interact with the dynamics of exploration (arXiv 2507.08210) and Lidayan et al. (2025) 2503.23631
finding: No study gives a rule for switching from information gain to entropy or empowerment. In Crafter, only entropy and empowerment tracked human exploration progress, with state diversity more useful early and control later (Lidayan, opened earlier as b15). In a tabular grid world, prioritising both curiosity and competence improved exploration over either alone (2507.08210, abstract).
numbers: No numbers read for 2507.08210.
limits: Abstract only for 2507.08210. Grid-world RL agents, not LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open. Working rule: use information gain while a code-countable rule list has more than one live member; when the list is empty or unbounded, use diversity first and control later. This is a design guess from two sources, not a tested switch.
